To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

attentional selection of visual input in the primate brain leads to a shift of the receptive fields of cortical neurons toward the attended location and to a small amount of receptive field shrinkage around the attended stimulus.

spatial attention alters receptive field profiles by dynamic shifts of their centers and small amounts of shrinkage, even far outside the current focus of spatial attention, and that these changes are already present in area MT, an extrastriate visual cortical area.
spatial attention in extrastriate visual cortex is associated with a shift of receptive field centers toward the attended location, and with a small amount of receptive field shrinkage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the brain processes information about the environment.
the neural basis of selective attention.
the neural mechanisms of attention and visual perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attention shifts receptive fields in MT and that this shift is a function of distance from the attended location.
attention is a dynamic, top-down process which is able to modulate the receptive field properties of cortical neurons in a way that is beneficial for visual perception.
the receptive fields of MT neurons do not shift in the presence of spatial attention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spatial attention in area MT is characterized by the dynamic shifts of receptive fields and the shrinkage of receptive fields.

attention is a top-down mechanism that dynamically alters the receptive field properties of neurons in extrastriate cortical areas, and this alteration is reflected by the changes in the neuronal response to visual stimuli.
attentional modulation is not limited to the area of the receptive field of the neuron but is a global modulation of the neuronal activity in the area of the visual cortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the receptive fields in the brain are not fixed, but rather they are highly modifiable and dynamic.
attention can change the receptive fields of cortical neurons.
attention can shift receptive field centers, even in the presence of a large stimulus, and this shift is independent of the size of the stimulus.
